title: Connecting the Dots: A Series on Multi-Tiered System of Supports (MTSS) at My School — Tiers 2 and 3
author: Elana
summary: In this installment of her mini-series on Multi-Tiered Systems of Support, Elana diagnoses two specific implementation failures common in schools running MTSS without clear protocols. The first is treating 'Tier 2' and 'Tier 3' as fixed labels rather than fluid levels of intensity, so that any student pulled by a reading interventionist gets automatically classified as Tier 3 regardless of actual need. The second, illustrated through detailed first-grade and fifth-grade data examples, is grouping students with similar composite scores together even when their subskill profiles are entirely different — a student who can decode but lacks fluency needs a different intervention than one who can't yet blend sounds, even if both score 'well below' on the same universal screener. Elana argues this data-blind grouping wastes intervention capacity and fails the students with the most acute needs. The piece closes on the underdeveloped side of MTSS: fading support once students show accelerated progress, arguing schools too often exit students from intensive intervention abruptly rather than planning a gradual, team-monitored reduction in support.
points: MTSS breaks down in practice when schools use Tier 2/3 as fixed labels instead of protocols: any student seeing a reading interventionist gets lumped into 'Tier 3' regardless of whether their actual need is Tier 2 intensity.

The first-grade case study shows why composite scores alone mis-group students: a child who can read connected text but lacks fluency needs different instruction than a child who cannot yet blend sounds, even though both score 'well below.'

The fifth-grade case study (one student reading at 53% accuracy with only 10 words at BOY) illustrates how limited interventionist capacity forces schools to group students of very different severity together, diluting support for the neediest.

Elana's most actionable point may be the most overlooked one: schools rarely plan how to fade intervention support once a student exits, and abrupt drop-off from five-days-a-week to none risks losing gains — a team should plan and monitor the fade, not just the entry.
quotes: A multi-tiered system of supports framework is designed to provide layers of intensified support for students who are not responding to explicit and systematic core instruction.

What ends up happening is that any student who receives intervention from a reading interventionist is identified as receiving Tier 3 support. Often, we start students with the heaviest amount of support, such as 5 days a week for 30 minutes of intervention with an integrated program like UFLI, Phonics for Reading, EBLI, and other intervention programs.

A student who can read some connected text at the beginning of first grade is very different from a student who can not read any words at all. At my school, these two students might land in the same intervention group, both labeled as receiving Tier 3 supports and the same intervention.

This student is a 5th grader who is reading with 53% accuracy and only 10 words at the beginning of 5th grade. This student might require increased dosage, but when too many students qualify for interventions, interventionists in a school setting can rarely dedicate additional periods to provide intensified instruction for this student.

It is unfair to expect students to go from intensive 5 day a week interventions to little to no support at all. A team of educators should be responsible for carefully and intentionally planning how supports are faded and whether a student is successful once supports are removed.

If students can maintain their success and data reflects progress, teams should proceed with exiting the student. If the student begins to regress or needs more support, teams should be ready to reinstall their intervention support.
